The Prophet ﷺ sent Mus'ab back with them to teach them the Qur'an. He was the first envoy of Islam.

It was a delicate mission. He was a stranger in a divided city, and he came with no army and no wealth. In Yathrib he stayed with As'ad ibn Zurara and taught patiently.

Then came the test. Two clan leaders, Usayd ibn Hudayr and Sa'd ibn Mu'adh, came one after the other intending to stop him. He invited each to sit and listen first. Both accepted Islam, and many of their people followed.

A year later, more than seventy men and women from Yathrib came to Mecca to pledge their support to the Prophet ﷺ. The city was ready to welcome him. Soon after, the migration to Medina began.

At Uhud, a mountain just north of Medina, the Muslims faced a Meccan army that had come to avenge its defeat at Badr the year before. Mus'ab was killed there in 625, carrying the Muslims' banner. His companions related that the only cloth they had for his shroud was too short to cover him completely: if they covered his head, his feet were bare. The Prophet ﷺ is reported to have had them cover his head with the cloth and put fragrant grass on his feet. The man who had once worn the finest clothes in Mecca left the world with almost nothing, and the city he had taught became the home of Islam.
lesson: Gentleness opens doors that force cannot. When someone comes to you angry, invite them to sit and listen first; patience and good manners are often the strongest argument.

title: Al-Biruni Measures the Earth From a Mountain
period: Ghaznavid Empire, Central Asia and India
teaser: On a height in what is now Pakistan, a scholar aims an instrument at the horizon, meaning to measure the whole Earth with one mountain and some geometry. How can a tiny angle reveal the size of a planet?
story:
On a height near the fort of Nandana, in what is now Pakistan, a scholar aims his instrument at the horizon. With one mountain and some geometry, he intends to measure the whole Earth.

Abu Rayhan al-Biruni was born in 973 in Khwarazm, in Central Asia. In the early eleventh century he came to India in the wake of the armies of Sultan Mahmud of Ghazni. While others looked for treasure, he looked for knowledge: he studied Sanskrit, talked with Indian scholars and wrote a large, fair-minded book, the Kitab al-Hind, describing India's sciences, beliefs and customs. He tried to present what Indians themselves believed and wrote, and not what outsiders said about them.

His idea at Nandana was elegant. First he measured the height of the mountain, by taking two sightings of its summit from two points on the plain. Then, from its top, he measured how far the horizon dipped below a level line. That angle is tiny, a fraction of a degree. But from that small angle and the mountain's height, trigonometry gave him the radius of the Earth. Why did it matter? To find the distance between two cities, or the direction of Mecca from a distant land, a geographer needs to know how big the Earth is. Al-Biruni cared about such questions, and he recorded his method in his astronomical writings.

Converted into modern units, his result is usually reckoned to be within about one or two per cent of today's value, though the exact length of his unit is uncertain.

It was a bold shortcut. About two centuries earlier, scholars working for the caliph al-Ma'mun had measured the Earth by having teams measure out long distances across the plains of Iraq. Al-Biruni's method needed only a mountain, an instrument and careful observation. Scholars of his time had inherited Greek geometry and trigonometry and developed both further, and his method rests on that tradition.

He was a scholar of many interests, writing on astronomy, mathematics, geography, medicine, minerals and history. He left behind well over a hundred works, most of them now lost. He is said to have kept working into old age, and he died around 1048.
lesson: A good method is worth more than great resources. Before saying a task is too big for you, look for the clever angle from which it becomes possible.

title: Khudadad Khan: The Sepoy Who Kept Firing
teaser: In October 1914 a wounded sepoy kept his machine gun firing until the other men of his detachment had been killed. Overrun and left among the fallen, what did he do when night came?
story:
In October 1914, the Indian Army had only just arrived in Flanders, in time to help hold the line near Ypres. The men were from the Punjab, Baluchistan and many other regions, and a large share of them were Muslims. They had landed at Marseille a few weeks earlier and had crossed France to a flat, wet and cold land, to fight in a war they had not started. Their regiments were among the first Indian units to meet the Germans in battle.

One of them was Khudadad Khan, a sepoy of the 129th Duke of Connaught's Own Baluchis. He was born in 1888 in a village in the Punjab, in today's Pakistan, and he was twenty-six years old. His job was to serve a machine gun.

On 31 October 1914, near the village of Hollebeke in Belgium, German forces attacked in strength. The Baluchis had been rushed forward to help a hard-pressed British line. The line was thin, and its machine guns were vital. A German shell put one of the guns out of action. The British officer in charge of the detachment was wounded. The Germans pressed closer.

Khudadad Khan, himself wounded, stayed at his gun. The official citation says he kept it working until the other men of the detachment had been killed. Then the position was overrun. The attackers took him for dead, and he lay among the fallen. When night came, he crawled away and found his way back to his own regiment.

His stand is credited with helping to delay the German advance until reinforcements could arrive. For it, he was awarded the Victoria Cross, the highest British award for courage, announced in December 1914. He was the first native Indian soldier to receive it. He later returned home, rose to the rank of subedar, and lived a long life in his native Punjab until 1971.

More than a million Indian soldiers served overseas in the First World War, and more than seventy thousand did not come home. Many of them were Muslims. Few of their names became well known. Khudadad Khan's name is one that survived, and it reminds us that courage on that battlefield did not come from a single country or a single faith.
lesson: Courage belongs to no empire and no rank. We honour the past best when we remember the people who stood in the line and were almost forgotten.

title: Sinan, the Architect Who Kept Learning
teaser: He was about fifty when he became chief architect of the Ottoman Empire, an age when many careers wind down. His lasted another half-century: which of his works is said to be his masterpiece?
story:
He was about fifty when he was named chief architect of the Ottoman Empire, an age at which many careers are winding down. His would last another half-century.

Sinan was born around 1490 in a Christian village of central Anatolia. As a young man he was recruited into the sultan's service, became a Muslim and joined the Janissaries. On campaign from the Balkans to Iraq, he learned his craft the hard way, building bridges, fortifications and ships as a military engineer. Armies cannot wait for perfect plans: a bridge must carry the soldiers across the river, and it must be ready in time.

In 1539 Sultan Suleiman the Magnificent put him in charge of imperial building, at the head of a large office of masons, carpenters, engineers and draughtsmen. Sinan served three sultans, and the lists of his works drawn up in his own time count more than three hundred: mosques, schools, hospitals, baths, bridges, aqueducts. The great bridge over the Drina at Visegrad, in Bosnia, is credited to him. He also helped to reinforce Hagia Sophia with new buttresses.

Hagia Sophia, the great domed church of the Byzantines, by then a mosque, was the model that every Ottoman architect had to face. Sinan spent his career exploring how to cover a vast hall with a dome, so that the whole space could be seen at once, light and open. He tried different supports and different shapes in building after building.

He never stopped trying to do better. A saying long attributed to him calls the Şehzade Mosque in Istanbul the work of his apprenticeship, the Süleymaniye that of his journeyman years, and the Selimiye in Edirne, finished when he was in his eighties, his masterpiece.

The Selimiye's great dome rests on eight pillars above a hall flooded with light. The Süleymaniye, finished in 1557, is not only a mosque: its complex also held schools, a hospital, baths and a soup kitchen. Among Sinan's apprentices was Mehmed Agha, who later built the Blue Mosque of Istanbul. The Selimiye was built for Sultan Selim II between 1568 and 1574. Sinan died in 1588 and rests in a modest tomb he designed himself, beside the Süleymaniye. His buildings still mark the skylines of Istanbul, Edirne and many other towns.
lesson: It is never too late to begin, and never time to stop improving. Treat each thing you finish as a lesson for the next one.

title: Timbuktu, the City That Treasured Books
period: Mali and Songhai empires, West Africa
teaser: In sixteenth-century Timbuktu a visitor noted that handwritten books earned more profit than any other goods in the market. What did the people of the city do with them when armed conflict arrived in 2012?
story:
In sixteenth-century Timbuktu, on the southern edge of the Sahara, a visitor noted something that surprised him: among all the goods sold in the market, handwritten books brought in more profit than any other merchandise.

That visitor is known as Leo Africanus, and the city he described was at its height. Enriched by the trade in gold and salt, Timbuktu had become, under the Mali and then the Songhai empires, a city of scholars. The Songhai ruler Askia Muhammad, who had made the pilgrimage to Mecca in the 1490s, honoured learned men. Caravans from the north brought salt, and boats on the Niger brought goods from the south. Students came from elsewhere in West Africa to study. Around the mosques of the city, especially Sankore, teachers gave lessons in law, grammar, astronomy and medicine.

Books were imported across the desert, copied by hand and commented on by local authors, in Arabic and sometimes in African languages written in Arabic script. The most famous of these scholars, Ahmad Baba, who died in 1627, said that his library of about 1,600 volumes was smaller than those of others in his family. He had paid a price for his learning: after Morocco conquered the region in 1591, he was taken to Marrakesh, and returned to Timbuktu only years later.

The books survived because families kept them, generation after generation, in chests and in the rooms of old houses. The climate of the desert edge helped: dry air is kind to paper. Each family guarded its inheritance, and passed it from father to child. The manuscripts deal with religion, but also with astronomy, medicine, mathematics and poetry, and even with business contracts and letters. Timbuktu's old mosques and its tombs are today a World Heritage Site.

In 2012, when armed conflict reached the city, librarians and ordinary residents secretly carried a very large part of the manuscripts to safety, trunk by trunk. Estimates of the number of manuscripts held in the region run into the hundreds of thousands. They were moved in secret, hidden in houses, and carried south by road and river.

Timbuktu had grown rich on gold and salt. What its people chose to save, when danger came, was their books.
lesson: A community shows what it truly values by what it protects in hard times. Take care of books and of the knowledge handed down to you; they are an inheritance for those who come after.

title: Noor Inayat Khan: The Radio Operator Who Stayed
teaser: Paris, summer 1943: the network's wireless operators are being caught one by one, and one is still transmitting under the code name Madeleine. Why did she stay when London reportedly offered to bring her home?
story:
Paris, summer 1943. The German security services were closing in on a network of agents sent from Britain to support the French Resistance. Arrests were taking place week after week. One by one, the network's wireless operators were caught. One of them was still transmitting. She was a young woman who went by the code name Madeleine. Her real name was Noor Inayat Khan.

She had been born on 1 January 1914 in Moscow. Her father, Inayat Khan, was an Indian Sufi teacher and musician who taught a message of love and harmony. Her mother was American. The family moved to London, then to Paris, where Noor studied child psychology and music and wrote stories for children, and in 1939 a book of Jataka tales that she retold for children was published. Her father died in 1927, when she was a child.

When Germany occupied France in 1940, the family fled to Britain. Noor joined the Women's Auxiliary Air Force and trained as a wireless operator. Later the Special Operations Executive, the British service that supported resistance in occupied Europe, recruited her. She spoke fluent French. According to reports from her instructors, some doubted she was suited to this work, but she was sent all the same.

In June 1943, she was flown to France by a small plane, the first woman radio operator the service had sent to the field there. Within weeks, her network collapsed. London reportedly offered to bring her home. She chose to remain. For about three months, she sent and received messages from different places in Paris, moving often and carrying her transmitter in a suitcase.

She was arrested in October 1943 and held at the Gestapo headquarters in Paris. She tried to escape and was caught again. She was then sent to Germany and held in harsh solitary conditions. On 13 September 1944, she was taken to Dachau with three other women from the same service and executed. One witness is reported to have recalled her last word as liberty.

After the war, Britain awarded her the George Cross, and France the Croix de Guerre. A memorial to her stands in London, near the area where she once lived. She was a person raised in a tradition of peace who chose, at terrible risk, to stand against tyranny.
lesson: Faith in peace and the courage to resist injustice can live in the same heart. Her quiet bravery reminds us that conscience sometimes asks us to stay when it would be safer to leave.

title: Al-Idrisi Maps the World for a King
teaser: In Palermo in the 1140s, a Muslim scholar at a Christian king's court questions travellers and keeps only what the witnesses agree on. Could a map of the whole world be built from other people's eyes?
story:
Palermo, Sicily, in the 1140s. At the court of a Christian king, a Muslim scholar is gathering reports from travellers: where they have been, how many days separate one town from the next, what grows there and what is sold. The accounts are compared, and what the witnesses agree on is kept; what they contradict is set aside.

The king is Roger II, a Norman ruler. Sicily had been ruled by Muslims since the ninth century before the Normans conquered it in the eleventh. His island is home to Latin and Greek Christians, Muslims and Jews. His court is a place where Arabic, Greek and Latin are all heard, and where Arab craftsmen and scholars still work. The scholar is al-Idrisi, born around 1100 in Ceuta, on the coast of North Africa. He had studied in Cordoba and travelled in Spain and North Africa before coming to Sicily. Roger, a patron of learning, has asked him for nothing less than a description of the whole known world.

It was an enormous task. Al-Idrisi drew on the writings of earlier geographers, Greek and Muslim, and on the accounts of merchants, sailors and pilgrims who came to Palermo. Where they disagreed, he weighed their words. He was building a picture of the world out of other people's eyes.

The work took about fifteen years. It was completed in 1154, shortly before the king died. It is a great book of geography, often called the Book of Roger, which divides the world into seventy sections, each with its own map, from the Atlantic to China, seven climate zones of ten sections each, with notes on distances, products and customs. The maps place south at the top, as was common among Muslim mapmakers, so that Africa appears above Europe. They are schematic, not like modern maps, but they are rich in names, routes and distances.

Al-Idrisi also had a large map of the world engraved on silver, which has since been lost. He later wrote another geographical work for Roger's son, William I.

For a long time his work remained one of the most detailed descriptions of the world ever made. It was born of a simple method: ask, compare, verify.
lesson: Before repeating something, check it against more than one source. Reliable knowledge is built by asking, comparing and keeping only what holds up.

title: Ibn al-Nafis and the Path of the Blood
period: Ayyubid and Mamluk Syria and Egypt
teaser: In 1924 a young Egyptian doctor in Germany opened an old Arabic manuscript and found a discovery that history books credited to Europeans three centuries later. What had its author understood about the heart?
story:
In 1924, a young Egyptian doctor studying in Germany examined an old Arabic manuscript kept in Berlin, and found in it a discovery that the history books credited to Europeans of three centuries later. His name was Muhyi al-Din al-Tatawi, and he was preparing a study of Ibn al-Nafis at the University of Freiburg.

The author was Ibn al-Nafis. Born near Damascus around 1213, he studied medicine at the city's Nuri hospital and then settled in Cairo, where he became chief physician of Egypt. He is also said to have served as physician to the Mamluk sultan Baybars. Around 1242 he wrote a commentary on the anatomy in Ibn Sina's Canon, a book every doctor knew.

The problem he tackled was ancient. For more than a thousand years, doctors had followed the Greek physician Galen, who taught that blood passed from the right side of the heart to the left through invisible pores in the wall between them. Ibn Sina and others had repeated the idea. Ibn al-Nafis argued plainly that there are no such pores: the wall is solid.

If the blood cannot pass through the wall, where does it go? Blood from the right side, he wrote, must travel to the lungs, mix there with air, and return to the left side of the heart. He had described the circulation of blood through the lungs. He also wrote that the heart is nourished by the vessels that run over its surface, and not by the blood inside its chambers.

His insight seems to have been little noticed in his own time. In Europe, the circulation through the lungs was described again in the sixteenth century, by physicians such as Michael Servetus and Realdo Colombo, and in the following century William Harvey described the circulation of the blood through the whole body.

Ibn al-Nafis kept working and writing until his death in Cairo in 1288, and left his house and his books to the new Mansuri hospital. It took the eyes of a student, nearly seven centuries later, to bring his page back into the light.
lesson: Respecting your teachers does not mean repeating their mistakes. Say what the evidence shows, calmly and honestly, even if recognition comes late or never.

title: Yarmouk: Six Days of Dust and Discipline
teaser: For about six days in August 636 two armies strained against each other in the gorges of the Yarmouk, neither able to break the other. What finally gave way on the last day?
story:
August 636. Along the deep gorges of the Yarmouk river, south of the Golan heights, two armies face each other. One serves the Byzantine emperor Heraclius. The other follows the caliph Umar in Medina and is led in the field by Abu Ubayda ibn al-Jarrah and the veteran commander Khalid ibn al-Walid.

The Byzantine soldiers are not villains in this story. They came to defend provinces their empire had ruled for centuries, only a few years after a long and draining war against Persia that had ended in 628. Their army was a mixture of peoples, Armenians and Arab allies among them. The Muslim chroniclers describe it as the larger force, though no one knows the real numbers and modern historians are cautious about them.

One episode, reported by later chroniclers, shows the spirit of the campaign. As the imperial army gathered, the Muslim commanders are said to have withdrawn from Homs, a city that had made terms with them. They gave back the tax they had collected, explaining that they could no longer protect the people who had paid it. Whether every detail is exact or not, it was remembered as a point of honour: a promise to protect had a price, and it was to be returned if it could not be kept.

The battle itself lasted about six days. According to the sources, Khalid gathered his cavalry into a mobile force that could ride to wherever the line was weakening, instead of leaving the horsemen scattered along the front. For days neither side could break the other. Tired men on both sides held on, in the heat of summer, with little room to manoeuvre between the river valley and the surrounding hills.

On the last day, accounts describe a wind that blew dust into the faces of the Byzantine troops. The Muslim cavalry struck, separated the imperial horsemen from their infantry, and the line gave way. Many of the retreating soldiers are said to have been caught by the ravines and cliffs around the river. For the empire it was a crushing defeat, and the sources agree on that much.

The consequences were enormous. Heraclius left Syria, and within a few years the whole region, Jerusalem included, passed under Muslim rule. Historians count Yarmouk among the battles that changed the history of the Mediterranean world. Yet the details we remember best, the dust, the cavalry, the withdrawal from Homs, were written down generations later, and honest history says so.
lesson: Numbers alone do not decide a struggle: discipline, timing and the trust of those you lead count for more. And a promise kept when it is costly is worth more than a victory won by breaking it.

title: The Astrolabe-Maker of Aleppo
teaser: Nearly everything known about her fits in one line of a tenth-century book, and we are not even sure of her first name. Who was the woman who made astrolabes at the court of Aleppo?
story:
We do not know her first name for certain. We do not know when she was born or when she died. Nearly everything known about her fits in one line of a tenth-century book, and yet she has not been forgotten.

Around 987, a Baghdad bookseller named Ibn al-Nadim compiled a great catalogue of the books and scholars of his time. In his list of the makers of astrolabes he mentions a woman: al-Ijliya, daughter of the astrolabe-maker al-Ijli, who had trained under a master of the craft and worked at the court of Sayf al-Dawla, ruler of Aleppo in Syria from about 944 to 967. That is all. The name Mariam, by which she is widely known today, does not appear in that text, and none of her instruments is known to survive.

But the line says a lot. Sayf al-Dawla's court was famous for its poets and scholars, and to be employed there was an honour. Aleppo in those years was also a frontier city, defended by its ruler against the Byzantines, and a meeting place of poets such as al-Mutanabbi and of the philosopher al-Farabi. And an astrolabe was a precision tool: a brass disc engraved with a map of the sky, hung from a ring so that the user could hold it up and sight a star along its back, used to tell the time, find the direction of Mecca and measure the height of the stars. For a Muslim city, it answered practical questions: when is the hour of prayer, and in which direction should the believer face?

Think of what it took to make one. The craftsman had to calculate the lines for a given latitude, engrave them with a steady hand on a thin plate, and fit together several moving parts so that they turned smoothly. A small error could make the whole instrument useless. Making one required mathematics, astronomy and a skilled engraver's hand.

She did not invent it, as is sometimes claimed; it is far older. Her place in history is more modest, and more human: she was a woman who practised a demanding craft, and was good enough to work for a prince.

The single line that remembers her has done its work. Today, an asteroid bears her name.
lesson: Honesty about what we do not know is part of respecting the past. And remember that good work matters even when history keeps only one line about the person who did it.

title: Salah ad-Din Enters Jerusalem Without a Massacre
teaser: In October 1187 the people of Jerusalem remembered the massacre of 1099, and now Saladin's army stood at their walls. Would history repeat itself?
story:
October 1187. Inside the walls of Jerusalem, people are terrified. They remember what happened when the Crusaders took the city in 1099: its Muslim and Jewish inhabitants were massacred. Now the army of Salah ad-Din — Saladin, a name that means righteousness of the faith — surrounds them, and they expect the same.

The city is crowded. Refugees from the surrounding country have poured in, and few trained soldiers remain: much of the Crusader army had been destroyed at Hattin three months earlier. Saladin, sultan of Egypt and Syria, had spent years uniting those lands under his rule, and he had won that battle. His men besieged Jerusalem from the end of September and undermined a section of the northern wall. After a short siege, the city's defender, Balian of Ibelin, came out to negotiate.

The agreement reached was that the city would surrender without bloodshed, and that its inhabitants could buy their freedom for a fixed ransom and leave in safety. The Muslim chronicles give the sums as ten dinars for a man, five for a woman and one for a child.

On 2 October, Saladin's troops entered Jerusalem. There was no massacre. According to the chroniclers, Saladin posted guards to keep order in the streets and at the gates, and guards protected the departing columns on the road. The arrangement was not gentle for everyone: many who could not pay were taken into captivity, as was the custom of the age. But chroniclers on both sides record that Saladin and his brother freed large numbers of the poor without payment, the elderly among them.

The city's Muslim life resumed. The first Friday prayer in the al-Aqsa Mosque was held about a week later. The Church of the Holy Sepulchre was left standing, and Eastern Christians remained in the city.

The fall of the city shocked Europe and led to the Third Crusade, which did not recover Jerusalem. Even there, Saladin was long remembered as a chivalrous enemy who kept his word. Chroniclers relate that when he died in Damascus in 1193 he had given away so much that little was left in his treasury. The memory of that autumn shows that mercy was possible even after decades of bitter war.
lesson: Strength shows its true quality at the moment of victory. When you have the upper hand, keep your word and choose mercy over revenge.

title: Tariq ibn Ziyad: The Crossing of 711
teaser: Spring 711: a small force lands beneath a great rock whose name, Jabal Tariq, gave us the word Gibraltar. The famous tale of burned ships is missing from the earliest sources, so what do we actually know?
story:
Spring, 711. A fleet crosses the narrow strait between North Africa and Iberia. On board are soldiers sent by Musa ibn Nusayr, the Umayyad governor of Ifriqiya, under the command of his lieutenant Tariq ibn Ziyad, usually described as a man of Berber origin. Over the previous decades, Umayyad armies had advanced across North Africa all the way to the Atlantic coast, and the sources say that many of Tariq's soldiers were recruited from the Berber peoples of the region. They land beneath a great rock. In Arabic it would be called Jabal Tariq, the mountain of Tariq, and from that name comes the word Gibraltar.

That much is firmly documented. What came next depended on a kingdom in trouble. The Visigothic realm of Iberia was divided by rivalries over the crown, and King Roderic is reported to have been far in the north, dealing with a rebellion, when news of the landing reached him. He marched south in haste to meet the newcomers.

The armies met in July 711, in a battle traditionally placed near the river Guadalete, in the south of the peninsula. The sources are sparse and sometimes contradict one another, but they agree on the outcome. Roderic's army was defeated, and the king himself disappears from history. Nobody can say for certain how he died.

Tariq did not stop. He pushed north through the cities of the south and reached Toledo, the Visigothic capital. In 712 Musa crossed with reinforcements and continued the campaign. Within a few years most of the peninsula had come under a new authority, and the region later known as al-Andalus began its long story.

Now the legend. A famous tale says that Tariq burned his ships on the beach so that his men could only go forward, and that he gave a stirring speech about the enemy before them and the sea behind them. This is told in countless books. But the earliest sources we have do not contain it, and it appears in writing only centuries later. Historians treat it as a later embellishment, however good the story.

The documented history needs no decoration. A small expeditionary force, a divided kingdom, a rapid decision and a campaign that went much further than anyone could have planned. What began as an expedition became a settled society that would later produce the libraries of Cordoba and the palaces of Granada.
lesson: A good story is not always a true one, and careful readers keep the two apart. History is often moved less by legends than by timing, by small decisions and by the weaknesses of those who are about to fall.

title: The Taj Mahal: Grief Turned Into Marble
teaser: In 1631 an emperor lost his wife far from home, and the next year work began on her tomb. How did its builders make verses high on a wall look the same size from the ground?
story:
In 1631, in the middle of a military campaign, the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan lost his wife. Mumtaz Mahal, whose name means the chosen one of the palace, died giving birth to their fourteenth child. She was first buried at Burhanpur, and her body was later moved to Agra. The court chroniclers describe an emperor overcome by grief. She had accompanied him even on campaign, and her death came far from home.

The following year, on the bank of the river Yamuna at Agra, in northern India, work began on her tomb. Thousands of craftsmen and labourers took part. White marble was brought from Makrana, in Rajasthan, hundreds of kilometres away, and other stones came from farther still to be set into the walls. The main building rose in about a decade, and the whole complex, with its mosque, gateway and gardens, was complete by about 1653.

Everything in it is balance, and the white marble seems to change colour with the light of the day. The tomb rises from a platform with a slender minaret at each corner. The complex is today a World Heritage Site. The tomb stands at the end of a long garden divided by water channels, an image of the gardens of Paradise. You pass through a great gateway, and suddenly the white dome appears, framed by the arch. Verses of the Qur'an frame the great arches, designed by the calligrapher Amanat Khan.

He solved a subtle problem. Letters high on a wall look smaller from below. So the letters grow larger as they climb, so that from the ground they all seem the same size. Flowers of coloured stone are set into the marble, each petal cut and fitted by hand.

The architect of the whole is traditionally said to be Ustad Ahmad Lahori, though many hands shaped it. In his later years Shah Jahan was deposed by his son Aurangzeb and kept at Agra Fort, within sight of the tomb, it is said.

Shah Jahan died in 1666 and was buried beside his wife. The popular tale that the workers' hands were cut off so that they could never build its equal has no historical basis.
lesson: Sorrow can be turned into something that gives beauty to others. And before repeating a dramatic story, ask whether it is actually true.

title: Ibn Khaldun and the Science of Societies
teaser: In 1375 a tired statesman who had known both favour and prison shut himself in a small fortress in what is now Algeria to ask why kingdoms rise and fall. What answer did he find?
story:
In 1375, a tired statesman shut himself away in a small fortress in the countryside of what is now Algeria. He had served several courts, and had known both favour and prison. A tribe of the region sheltered him there for about four years. Now he wanted to understand: why do kingdoms rise, and why do they fall?

Ibn Khaldun was born in Tunis in 1332, into a family of Andalusian origin. As a teenager he lost his parents and several of his teachers to the Black Death. For some twenty years he lived the dangerous life of a court official, from Fez to Granada. He saw ministers fall overnight, rulers deposed or killed, and fortunes reversed. He spent time in prison himself.

In the fortress of Ibn Salama he began a history of the world, and completed the first draft of its introduction, the Muqaddima, in 1377. In it he asks historians to stop repeating tales and to check whether what they report is even possible. He studies how climate, work, trade, taxes and education shape societies. A ruler who raises taxes too high, he argues, discourages work and ends up with less. The introduction opens a larger history of the Arabs, the Berbers and their neighbours.

And he describes a force he calls asabiyya, the solidarity that binds a group together: strong among those who live a hard life, it lets them build a state, then fades with comfort, generation after generation. He reckoned that a dynasty rarely lasted much beyond three generations.

The scholar later settled in Cairo, where he taught and served several times as a judge, being dismissed and reappointed more than once. He tells that in 1401, when the conqueror Timur besieged Damascus, he was lowered by ropes over the city wall to meet him.

He kept revising the Muqaddima for years, and in his later years he wrote an autobiography. He argued that history should look not only at kings and battles but at how people make a living. He died in Cairo in 1406. Many see in him a forerunner of sociology and economics, a man who turned his own hard experience into a way of understanding history.
lesson: Step back from events to look for their causes. Whoever understands why things happen, instead of only what happened, is better prepared for what comes next.

title: Gallipoli: The Day the Guns Fell Silent
teaser: 24 May 1915, Gallipoli: soldiers walk out of their trenches carrying shovels, not weapons, and stand within a few steps of the men they have been fighting. Why have the guns fallen silent?
story:
24 May 1915, Gallipoli peninsula. The rifles are quiet. Along a narrow strip of broken ground, soldiers walk out of their trenches carrying shovels, not weapons. For the first time in weeks, Ottoman soldiers and the Australian and New Zealand troops they have been fighting stand within a few steps of each other.

The Allied landings had begun on 25 April. For the Ottoman side, defending the Dardanelles strait was a matter of survival, because the road to the capital, Istanbul, lay beyond it. Mustafa Kemal, then a lieutenant colonel commanding the 19th Division, rushed his men to the heights above the landing beaches and helped hold the ridges. A famous order is attributed to him that day, telling his soldiers that he was asking them not just to fight but to die in their places. The exact words are reported in different ways, so they are best treated as tradition rather than record.

On 19 May the Ottoman army launched a large counter-attack to push the invaders into the sea. It failed, at a terrible cost. Thousands of Ottoman soldiers were killed or wounded. Between the lines lay the fallen of both sides, in the warm weather of late spring, and the situation soon became unbearable for the living in the trenches.

The two sides agreed on a truce, arranged by officers carrying white flags, so that the dead could be buried. It lasted a single day. Men who had been shooting at each other gathered their dead, and some later wrote that the enemy's fallen were treated with respect. Several participants later wrote that soldiers exchanged cigarettes and small souvenirs. At the appointed hour the white flags came down, the men returned to their trenches, and the war resumed.

The campaign continued for months more and ended with the Allied evacuation at the turn of 1916. Many tens of thousands of men died on both sides. Decades later, a monument at Anzac Cove carries words attributed to Atatürk, addressed to the mothers of foreign soldiers who died there, telling them that their sons now rest in friendly soil. Historians debate how that text came to be attributed to him, yet the spirit of it was lived out by the soldiers of 1915 on that day of truce.
lesson: Even in the middle of a war, a shared duty to the dead can remind enemies of their common humanity. Courage on the battlefield is admirable; courtesy toward a fallen foe is what makes it noble.

title: Umar in Jerusalem: A City Handed Over in Trust
teaser: Jerusalem, around 637: under siege, its patriarch is said to offer the surrender of the city, but only to the caliph in person. What kind of ruler would make that journey, and what would he promise?
story:
Jerusalem, around 637 or 638. The city has been under siege for months. It holds some of the holiest places of Christianity, and its leader, the Patriarch Sophronius, knows that the walls will not hold forever. According to tradition, he makes an unusual offer: he will negotiate the surrender, but only with the caliph in person.

The caliph, Umar ibn al-Khattab, is in Medina, far away, at the head of a state that has expanded with astonishing speed. Tradition relates that he made the journey himself, travelling with a single attendant and taking turns with him on one mount, in simple clothes. The detail is reported by later historians, who loved it, but it fits the way Umar was remembered.

What mattered more was the agreement that was made. According to the historian al-Tabari, who preserved a text of it, Umar granted the people of Aelia, the name by which Jerusalem was then known, a pledge of safety for their lives, their property, their churches and their crosses. The churches were not to be taken over or damaged, and people were not to be forced to change their faith. As in other agreements of that time, the inhabitants were to pay a tax in return for protection. Scholars discuss the exact wording and the date of the text we have, but all agree that the city surrendered without being stormed.

A well-known anecdote, also related by tradition, concerns prayer. The patriarch invited Umar to pray inside the Church of the Holy Sepulchre. Umar declined and prayed outside, explaining that if he prayed within, later Muslims might claim the building as a mosque. A mosque named after Umar stands near the church to this day, a reminder of this story.

Umar also visited the Temple Mount, which was then littered with rubble, and tradition says Muslims helped to clear it. Decades later, under the Umayyads, the Dome of the Rock and the Aqsa Mosque were built there.

Whatever the details, the story endured because it offered a model: a ruler who is entrusted with a city, and who treats that trust as a responsibility rather than a prize. For the people of Jerusalem, a city without a massacre was no small thing.
lesson: Real power shows itself in the way it treats those who cannot resist. A written promise of safety, kept by those who give it, can protect a city better than walls.

title: Ibn Fadlan: A Caliph's Envoy on the Volga
teaser: In June 921 a small embassy left Baghdad for the far edge of the known world, answering a king's request. One member wrote down what he saw, even when he disliked it: what did he meet on the Volga?
story:
June 921, Baghdad. A small embassy sets out toward the north-east. It has been sent by the caliph al-Muqtadir in answer to a request from Almish, the king of the Volga Bulghars, who lived on the far edge of the known world. The king had asked for people to teach his subjects about Islam and for help in building a fortress, which is generally understood as protection against his powerful neighbours, the Khazars. One of the envoy's officials was a man named Ahmad ibn Fadlan.

The road was long and hard. The party travelled through Persia, passing cities such as Rayy and Nishapur, and on to Bukhara and then Khwarazm. There, winter caught them. Ibn Fadlan describes cold so fierce that rivers froze solid and travellers wrapped themselves in layers of furs. The caravan waited for the weather to ease before crossing the steppe, where they met the Oghuz Turks, a people they had never seen. Ibn Fadlan watched them closely and wrote down what surprised him, from their dress to their customs, not with scorn but with the curiosity of a reporter.

In May 922, the embassy reached the king. Ibn Fadlan delivered the caliph's letter and gifts, and read the letter before the assembled people. He records that the king took a new name, Jafar ibn Abdallah. The sources do not tell us how deep or how quickly the spread of Islam went there, and Ibn Fadlan himself is our main witness.

On the Volga, he also met merchants called the Rus, trading in furs and slaves. His description of them, written at length, is among the earliest eyewitness accounts of these people. He was no friend of some of their habits and said so, but he wrote what he saw rather than what he expected.

His report, the Risala, survived in only a few manuscripts. One was found in 1923 in Mashhad, by the scholar Zeki Velidi Togan. In modern times the tale reached readers and film audiences who had never heard of the original. We do not know how or when Ibn Fadlan returned, or where he died.

What remains most striking is the tone of the man: curious, observant, willing to put down what he saw, even when it challenged his own views.
lesson: Travel teaches best when we look before we judge. A curious, honest observer leaves the future more than his opinions: he leaves a true picture of the world as he found it.

title: Imam Shamil: A Mountain Leader and a Hostage Son
teaser: In 1859 a man in his sixties came down from his last mountain stronghold, after leading Dagestan and Chechnya against the Russian Empire for twenty-five years. What had it cost him, and what became of his hostage son?
story:
Gunib, in the highlands of Dagestan, 1859. A man in his sixties comes down from his last mountain stronghold to surrender. For twenty-five years Imam Shamil has led the peoples of Dagestan and Chechnya against the Russian Empire, and until this day he has never been captured.

Shamil was born in the village of Gimry, a scholar by training, and became the third imam of the mountain communities in 1834. He worked to unite valleys that were often divided, built a system of administration and courts based on Islamic law, and used the steep terrain with great skill. At the height of his power his imamate stretched across much of Dagestan and Chechnya. Again and again, much larger forces failed to pin him down.

The war cost him dearly. In 1839, after the siege of the fortress of Akhulgo, Shamil escaped but his young son Jamaleddin, about nine years old, was handed over to the Russians as a hostage. The boy was raised far away, in the imperial capital, in a world very different from the mountains.

In 1854, Shamil's fighters raided Tsinandali, in Georgia, and captured several women and children of princely families, among them Princess Anna Chavchavadze and Princess Varvara Orbeliani. They were held for months in the mountains. Accounts left by the prisoners describe an anxious captivity, yet they also suggest that they were treated with courtesy by Shamil's household. In 1855 an exchange was arranged: the captives went home, and Jamaleddin was returned to his father, along with a ransom.

At Gunib in 1859 the end came, when Russian forces surrounded the last stronghold. Shamil surrendered and was received with a respect that surprised many. Tsar Alexander II met him, and he lived in Russia under supervision for years, first in Kaluga. In 1870 he was allowed to make the pilgrimage to Mecca, and he died in Medina in 1871, where he is buried.

Historians still debate his rule, as with any leader of a long war. Some stress the heavy demands his state placed on mountain villages, others his learning, his discipline and his refusal to give up. Even his adversaries wrote of his endurance, and in Dagestan and across the Caucasus he is remembered as a symbol of resistance.
lesson: Even in a long and bitter war, accounts of decency toward captives deserve to be remembered, and so does the plain fact that both sides took hostages, children included. Endurance and mercy are best judged side by side.

title: Piri Reis and the Map on Gazelle Skin
teaser: In 1513 a sea captain bent over gazelle skin to draw the Atlantic from about twenty sources, one a chart he says came from a man who sailed with Columbus. How did the map vanish, and where was it found?
story:
Gallipoli, 1513. A sea captain bends over a sheet of gazelle skin, a brush in his hand. His name is Piri, later known as Piri Reis, the captain. Born in the Dardanelles port of Gallipoli around 1470, he learned the sea as a young man at the side of his uncle, the admiral Kemal Reis, and sailed the length of the Mediterranean.

Now he is trying something rare in the Ottoman world: to draw the Atlantic. The Portuguese had rounded Africa, and Columbus had crossed the ocean, and Piri wanted to put it all on one sheet. In the notes on the map he wrote that he had combined about twenty sources: Greek, Arabic, Indian and Portuguese charts, and a map used by Columbus, which he says came from a man who had sailed with him. It is the kind of source list a modern historian would ask for.

The map he finished is vivid. The coasts of Iberia and West Africa are drawn with confidence, crossed by the web of compass lines typical of the sea charts of that age. Across the ocean he placed the new lands, with the Caribbean islands and the coast of South America, decorated with ships, animals and short notes in Ottoman Turkish. Only the western part of the world map survives, but it is one of the oldest surviving maps to show the Americas.

In 1517, tradition says, Piri presented it to Sultan Selim I in Cairo, after the Ottoman conquest of Egypt. After that it disappeared. It was rediscovered in 1929, when a German scholar named Gustav Adolf Deissmann found it in the Topkapi Palace library while the palace was being converted into a museum.

Piri Reis also wrote the Kitab-i Bahriye, a book of sailing directions for the Mediterranean ports, still admired for its detail. His own end was unhappy: after a failed naval campaign in the Gulf he was executed in about 1553.

In recent decades many popular claims have grown around the map, about lost civilisations and impossible knowledge. Historians find no support for these. The truth is more impressive: a patient scholar who compared charts from many cultures and put the pieces together.
lesson: Knowledge grows when people are willing to learn from every source, whatever its language or origin. Real discovery is often patient comparison before it is a flash of genius.

title: Rufayda al-Aslamiyya and the Tent of Healing
teaser: Medina, 627: with enemy tribes outside the city, a wounded leader is taken to a tent beside the mosque. Whose tent was it, and why do some modern writers call her the first Muslim nurse?
story:
Medina, 627. Enemy tribes are gathered outside the city, and a long trench protects the open side. The days are tense. Arrows still fly across the ditch from time to time, and some men come back wounded. One of them is Sa'd ibn Mu'adh, a leader of the Ansar, who has been struck in the arm. Where can he be treated?

Tradition relates that the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ had him placed in a tent set up beside the mosque, so that he could be visited and watched over closely. The tent belonged to a woman named Rufayda bint Sa'd, of the Aslam tribe, known in the sources as Rufayda al-Aslamiyya. Later biographers add that she had learned the care of the wounded, and that her father was a physician from whom she picked up her skills. In the tent she and other women looked after the sick and injured.

It is not easy to say how much of her story we know. The sources about her are short, and some details come to us from later writers. But the early sources, such as the biographical dictionary of Ibn Sa'd and the biography of Ibn Ishaq, say little more than this: a woman whose tent beside the mosque served as a place where the wounded were treated. Some modern writers call her the first Muslim nurse.

Later writers add that she is said to have trained young women in nursing, to have cared for orphans and the poor who had nobody to look after them, and to have gone out with expeditions to attend the wounded. In the same way, the sources mention other women who gave first aid and carried water to the injured in the early battles.

The wounded man she treated did not survive his injury for long, as his wound proved fatal. But what she created lasted longer than he did: the idea that care for the sick is a service to be organised, trained and shared, and that a tent beside the mosque can serve as a place of healing as well as prayer.

Centuries later, great hospitals in Baghdad, Cairo and Damascus would carry the care of the sick much further, though they grew from many sources.
lesson: One person who sets up a place of care can start something that grows far beyond her.

title: Cut Nyak Dhien: The Widow Who Led the Aceh Forests
teaser: Around 1900 a woman in her fifties, nearly blind and in pain, still led a band of fighters through the forests of Aceh. According to Indonesian tradition, one of her own men led the Dutch to her camp: why?
story:
Aceh, northern Sumatra, around 1900. A woman in her fifties, nearly blind and suffering from pains in her joints, moves through the forest with a handful of loyal fighters. The Dutch have been at war with Aceh for more than a quarter of a century. Her name is Cut Nyak Dhien, and she is one of the few leaders who has still not laid down arms.

She was born in 1848 into a family of Acehnese nobles, raised in a society where religious learning mattered a great deal. When the Dutch attacked Aceh in 1873, the war began that would last for decades. In 1878 her first husband, Teuku Ibrahim Lamnga, was killed in battle. Some years later she married Teuku Umar, a bold commander, who continued the fight.

Teuku Umar became famous for a bold trick. In 1893 he appeared to submit to the Dutch, accepted a command, and received weapons and supplies. A few years later, in 1896, he turned back to the Acehnese cause with the arms he had been given. In 1899 he was killed in an ambush near Meulaboh. Cut Nyak Dhien, instead of withdrawing, took up the leadership of his guerrilla band and kept the resistance going in the hills and forests for years.

Time and hardship wore her down. By 1905 she was elderly, in poor health, and struggling to feed her people. According to Indonesian tradition, one of her own men, Pang Laot, grew so worried about her condition that he led the Dutch to her camp, hoping she would receive treatment. She was captured that year. Reports say that she continued to rebuke him as a traitor, and the memory of this moment is told in Aceh with some sadness.

The Dutch exiled her to Sumedang, in West Java, far from home. There she lived quietly in the household of a local religious figure and taught the Qur'an to the neighbourhood women. Local people called her Ibu Perbu, the Lady Queen. Tradition holds that the authorities kept her identity hidden to prevent her from becoming a rallying point, and that many neighbours learned who she was only after her death in November 1908.

In 1964 Indonesia named her a National Hero. Her tomb in Sumedang is still visited today, a reminder that the forest fighter and the village teacher were the same woman.
lesson: Courage can survive the loss of everything: family, health and homeland. And some people go on serving their community in quiet ways, long after the world has stopped watching.

title: Ja'far in the Court of the Negus
teaser: Around 615 a small group of Muslims crossed the Red Sea in secret, and Quraysh sent envoys with gifts to bring them back. Would a Christian king hand them over?
story:
Around the year 615, a small group of Muslims leaves Mecca in secret and crosses the Red Sea. They are fleeing persecution at home, and the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ has advised them to seek refuge in Abyssinia, where, tradition relates, he told them a king rules who does not wrong anyone. The king is the Negus, a Christian ruler of the kingdom of Aksum.

The refugees settle and find, for the first time in years, peace to practise their faith. But the leaders of Quraysh do not intend to let this go. According to the early biographers, they send two envoys, Amr ibn al-As and Abdullah ibn Abi Rabia, carrying gifts for the king and for his court officials. The plan is to persuade the officials in advance, then ask the king to hand the Muslims back.

Tradition relates, through an account attributed to the Companion Umm Salama, who was among the refugees, what happened next. The Negus decided not to rule on the matter without hearing the Muslims themselves. He summoned them and asked what this new religion was that had made them leave their people. The man chosen to speak for the group was Ja'far ibn Abi Talib, a cousin of the Prophet ﷺ.

Ja'far, the sources say, explained how their community had lived before: in ignorance, idol worship and the abuse of the weak. Then a messenger had come from among them, known for honesty, calling them to worship One God, to tell the truth, to keep family ties and to protect neighbours. For this, they had been persecuted. When asked to share something of what the Prophet ﷺ had brought, Ja'far recited a passage about Mary from the Qur'an. The accounts report that the king and his bishops were moved to tears.

The Negus refused to hand the Muslims over. The envoys tried again on the following day with another argument, but the king once more heard the Muslims and held his ground. The envoys left with their gifts and their plan in ruins.

The refugees remained under his protection for years. Ja'far and others rejoined the Prophet ﷺ in Medina around the time of Khaybar, in the year 628 or 629. It is a story about a king who listened, a speaker who was honest and calm, and a faith that found, in a foreign court, a hospitality that its own city had refused.
lesson: Telling the truth calmly, with respect for the one who listens, can win more than any gift or pressure. And a fair ruler is one who hears both sides before he decides.

title: A Mosque in Surrey for Soldiers Far From Home
teaser: Woking, 1915: a domed building in the style of Mughal architecture stands among English pines, almost empty for years. How did it become a place of farewell for soldiers from the other side of the world?
story:
Woking, Surrey, 1915. An elegant domed building, built in the style of Mughal architecture, stands among English pine trees. Few people could have predicted that it would become a place of farewell for soldiers from the other side of the world.

The Shah Jahan Mosque had been built in 1889 by a scholar named Gottlieb Leitner, with funds from Shah Jahan, the Begum of Bhopal, in India. It is generally regarded as the first purpose-built mosque in Britain. After Leitner's death it fell into disuse, and for years it stood almost empty.

Then came the First World War. Soldiers of the Indian Army, many of them Muslims, Sikhs and Hindus, were sent to the Western Front in 1914 and fought in some of the first battles of the war, in cold and mud that were nothing like their homes. The wounded were brought to hospitals in southern England, including a large hospital in Brighton set up in the Royal Pavilion and other buildings. The authorities tried to respect the faith of their patients, preparing food according to religious needs and allowing space for prayer.

For Muslim soldiers, the mosque at Woking was brought back into use. Eid prayers were held there. And when men died of their wounds, a burial ground was opened in 1915 close by, on Horsell Common, so that they could be buried according to Islamic rites, their graves facing Mecca. Imams led the funeral prayers. Hindu and Sikh soldiers who died in Brighton were cremated on the Sussex Downs, where a memorial called the Chattri was later raised in their memory. A commemoration is still held there each year.

In 1968, the Muslim graves were moved to Brookwood Cemetery nearby, where the soldiers still rest today. A visitor can find them there, each marked with a name and regiment. The mosque in Woking, restored long ago, is still in use.

These men had come from villages in Punjab and other parts of India to a war that was not of their making, in a country where they knew almost no one. The simple fact that a mosque could be opened for them, and that someone remembered to turn their graves toward Mecca, says something about the dignity owed even to strangers.
lesson: A person's last journey deserves care, no matter where they come from. Remembering the forgotten, including those who served in wars far from their homes, is a duty of the living.

title: The Hijaz Railway: Pilgrims on Rails
teaser: In 1900 the pilgrim road from Damascus to Medina meant about forty days of heat and danger. Could a railway, backed by donations from India to North Africa, cut that to a few days?
story:
Damascus, 1900. For centuries, the pilgrim caravan has left this city each year toward the holy cities of Arabia. The trip across the desert is slow, hot and dangerous. Travellers fall ill, supplies run short, and some pilgrims never come home. The journey to Medina takes about forty days.

That year the Ottoman sultan Abdulhamid II announced a project that many thought too ambitious: a railway of about 1,300 kilometres, running from Damascus south to Medina, to carry pilgrims in comfort and in days instead of weeks. It would also help the empire carry mail, goods and soldiers to its distant provinces.

The money was a challenge. The Ottoman treasury was under strain, and the project was presented as a gift of the Muslim community. Donations came from places as far apart as India and North Africa, along with contributions from Ottoman officials, special stamps and taxes. Many ordinary people gave what they could, and the project was presented as being built without foreign loans. Even so, the state carried much of the cost.

Building it was a feat of engineering. The workers laid track through the rocky and waterless country of the Hejaz. The chief engineer was a German, Heinrich August Meissner, who worked together with Ottoman engineers, and a very large share of the labour was carried out by Ottoman soldiers. Water had to be brought to the work camps and stations, and fortified stations were built along the line to protect it. Work advanced a few kilometres at a time, with each stretch opened to traffic as it was finished.

The line reached Medina in 1908. A pilgrim who once needed more than a month could now travel from Damascus in about four or five days. A beautiful station was built in Medina to welcome them. A branch line to the Mediterranean port of Haifa, opened in 1905, linked the railway to the sea. The planned extension to Mecca was never built.

Then the First World War came, and parts of the track were damaged in the fighting and never fully restored. Today, sections survive, and old locomotives and stations can still be seen in Damascus, Amman and Medina. The railway's working life was short, but its story shows what a large community can do when it pools small gifts for one purpose.
lesson: Great undertakings are often built from many small contributions. When a whole community gives a little, something nobody could do alone becomes possible.
